items.title: Ryanair says it may freeze workers' pay and raise airfares
items.summary: The airline says fuel prices may rise by €2bn in 2028 unless there is an end to the US-Israel war with Iran.
items.content:
By Mitchell Labiak ,Â  Business reporter Â  and Â  Theo Leggett ,Â  Business correspondent
Ryanair is considering a temporary wage freeze for staff and confirmed airfares will be "materially higher" next summer because of a sharp rise in fuel costs following the US-Israel war with Iran.
The airline said it expects fuel prices to remain high "well into 2027" unless there is a "swift resolution" to the conflict.
Ryanair said its fuel bill is forecast to be â¬2bn (Â£1.6bn) higher in the short-term and its boss, Michael O'Leary, said airfares would have to rise by "double-digits" to help cover the cost.
But the firm said that was unlikely to be enough and it is looking into pay freezes. Unite, the union representing Ryanair staff, said it had not been told of "any such proposals".
O'Leary also said the company would slow down hiring as airline's costs rise.
The airline said its pre-tax profits fell by 16% to â¬2.4bn during the six months to the end of September, largely due to fuel costs jumping by 15%.
The company said that although 80% of its fuel bill had been "hedged" â in effect, bought in advance at fixed prices â the cost of the remainder was elevated.
O'Leary reiterated forecasts from earlier this year Ryanair would "need a 20% fare increase" to cover the cost of jet fuel.
"I'm not sure we'll get to 20%," he said. "But we're certainly looking at double-digit fare increases across Europe from all airlines in 2027."
Aviation fuel prices have surged this year as a result of the US-Israel war with Iran, which has dramatically reduced the supply of refined products coming from the Gulf and increased competition for those produced elsewhere.
Ryanair also said it was weighing up whether to freeze pay, as multi-year wage deals with unions come to to an end. The policy could be implemented from April next year.
Oliver Richardson, national officer at Unite, said the union "hasn't been advised of any such proposals and we have a multi-year pay deal in place which covers next year. A number of Unions across Europe have the same".
He said: "Our pay agreement was not attached to, nor dependent on company performance. This was something that the Ryanair was at pains to emphasise. As such we would expect it to be honoured."
Ryanair also said it would increase its use of artificial intelligence within its back office and support functions.
Meanwhile, Ryanair has cut back on winter flights and said on Monday there would be more to come. It said this was happening across the airline industry, particularly with short-haul carriers.
O'Leary said: "We believe those cuts will continue into the summer of 2027. Over the medium term, we expect short-haul capacity will remain constrained out to the early 2030s."

Supermarkets across Europe have experienced temperature-control meddling

Freezers are emptied and frozen goods are loaded into shopping carts to be thrown away at ICA Kvantum in Sjöbo, Sweden. Photograph: Johan Nilsson/TT/Shutterstock
I’m going to leave the blog there for now, here’s what you need to know:
Supermarket chains across Europe are dealing with another wave of cyber-attacks on their refrigeration systems after hackers managed to get into the temperature controls, turning the dial past 50C, spoiling huge quantities of frozen and fresh produce
The temperature tampering was reported by chains across Belgium, Luxembourg, Sweden, Ireland and Estonia and affected Spar, Delhaize, Coop, ICA, Carrefour and SuperValu supermarkets among others as well as an Ikea store’s freezers in Belgium
This is the second wave of attacks on such a scale targeting fridge and freezer controls following a cyber-hack of more than 700 supermarkets in France last month. Dutch supermarkets were also affected then.
It’s still unclear who or which group is responsible for the latest incidents; if they’re from the same perpetrators of the French attack or if it’s a copycat operation
But the EU food commissioner said it was aimed at undermining consumer confidence in the bloc’s food supply
Fewer stores were affected in this round compared to the French cyber-hack, and for most of the chains it was only a minority of stores that were affected
Swedish retailer Coop said it did use Danfoss systems in some of its affected stores – the same Danish system that was targeted in the French supermarchés last month.
Swedish supermarket employees chuck out spoiled food at an ICA Kvantum supermarket in Sjoebo, Sweden on November 2, 2026 after a hacker attack raised the temperature in the freezers to 50 degrees Celcius. Photograph: Johan Nilsson/TT NEWS AGENCY/AFP/Getty Images

The hacking of supermarket fridges and freezers has affected more than 100 stores at last count across Europe , reports AFP news agency.
In Belgium, Luxembourg, Sweden, Ireland and Estonia, supermarkets and retailers have had to throw away vast quantities of spoiled food.
Below is a list of affected retailers and what they’ve said on the incident, helpfully compiled by AFP.
The Dutch supermarket operator said an overnight “IT incident” affected fridges and freezers at dozens ⁠of Delhaize stores in Belgium and Luxembourg.
The chain detected temperature rise in its ​cooling systems on Monday and is ‌investigating.
Ahold also reported a cybersecurity incident to Dutch police last month after ‌detecting suspicious activity in its infrastructure.
The French retailer said about 15 of its 700 Belgian locations were impacted by refrigeration problems.
The company runs Spar stores in Belgium as franchises and said five shops had their fridge systems attacked.
Swedish Coop said cooling systems ‌at seven of its 800 stores were affected, with disruptions ranging from complete shutdowns to partial operation. It confirmed that ​the issues were a result of a cyber incident involving unauthorized tampering with the cooling systems. It said Danish company Danfoss was among its suppliers.
The Belgian butchery chain’s store in Hove, south of Antwerp, found its fridges ⁠turned up as high as 18 degree Celsius, ruining about €15,000 ($16,764) worth ​of meat, founder Luc ​De Laet said.
Privately held ​ICA said a limited number of stores were affected by ​an overnight incident ‌hitting their refrigeration and ​freezer systems.
The ​food wholesaler said a cyber incident had affected refrigeration systems in 13 of its SuperValu stores in Ireland , forcing it to remove some chilled and frozen products from sale.
The information we’re getting about how the cyber-attack occurred is still piecemeal; but we’re getting more details from from different affected supermarket chains.
In Sweden, the Coop supermarket chain just released a statement confirming a cyber incident involving “unauthorised tampering” in their fridge’s cooling systems.
Noticeably, Coop also confirmed that one of their system suppliers is Danfoss , the same Danish company which supplied temperature controllers to the French supermarkets attacked last month.
In the French attack, the hackers pirated controllers that were mostly supplied by Danfoss . They disabled the alarm systems before adjusting the thermostats or extending the defrost programme by hours.
Several of the affected supermarket chains today say that fridge and freezer temperatures were pushed to 50C. From the incident in Estonia, we know too that the computer programme controlling the temperature controls was hacked into, according to authorities there.
An Irish shopper looks at an empty refrigerator at a SuperValu supermarket affected by Monday’s hacks. Photograph: Reuters Given the geographic scale of this latest wave of fridge cyber-attacks – with stores in Belgium, Luxembourg, Sweden, Estonia and Ireland all affected- it’s worth remembering the recent warnings from governments urging citizens to prepare food and water stockpiles.
Just a fortnight ago, the UK government blasted out its ‘Be Ready’ campaign , urging households to be prepared with three days’ worth of food and water (about nine litres per person) at home, in case of emergencies.
Fridge hacking wasn’t put down as a reason – the first known incidents of this type on this scale, were only reported in France in October. But there has been growing official concerns about the impact of the climate crisis, technological dependency and hostile state threats.
The EU food commissioner has said that the bloc’s food security isn’t in question, but these latest fridge attacks will be another wake-up call for citizens.
An empty freezer in a Delhaize supermarket in Boortmeerbeek, Belgium with a sign reading "Due to cyberattacks, there will be no products available in the refrigerators/freezers. Our sincere apologies." Photograph: Maude Brulard/AFP/Getty Images This latest wave of cyberattacks targeting supermarkets across Europe is “a deliberate attempt to ⁠disrupt” the EU’s food supply, says Christophe Hansen, the European ‌Commissioner for Agriculture and Food.
He added it was also aimed at undermining the public’s confidence, and while “food security is not ⁠currently at risk, ... ​the food ​waste ​and impact ​on ‌businesses ​are ​real.”
The Swedish furniture giant is the latest to report that its stores have also been affected – saying at least one store in Belgium was targeted.
The home retailer specified it was a store in Mons, that had also suffered an attack on its refrigeration control systems. (Think of the meatballs!)
Belgium supermarkets this morning had already reported the breaches, affecting dozens of stores including Spar, Carrefour and Delhaize sites.
Ikea said it had been forced to remove some food from their fridges as a precaution.
“We cannot rule ​out ​that additional ​locations may be affected, ​as ‌we ​continue ​our investigation,” an IKEA spokesperson said.
Reuters has a quick snap that an EU spokesperson has said it will continue to work with member states over the fridge and freezer cyber-attacks reported earlier .
The spokesperson insisted the EU had several tools in place to deal with such incidents, but that it showed that cyber-attacks can disrupt the daily lives of citizens.
A notice informing customers that refrigerators are temporarily out of service in Linkebeek near Brussels, Belgium. Photograph: Stéphanie Lecocq/Reuters Three men accused of causing a deadly explosion in the heart of Athens’ tourist district by allegedly stealing copper piping from the local gas supply network were appearing in court Monday for a preliminary hearing, AP reports.
The September blast killed six people when it caused the collapse of a two-story residential building in the Greek capital’s historic Plaka district, near the ancient Acropolis. The three suspects allegedly removed piping from the building’s gas supply network to sell the copper as scrap, and face charges including arson, manslaughter with possible intent, causing a deadly explosion and causing dangerous bodily harm.
Firefighters attend the aftermath of the September gas explosion in Athens that killed six. Photograph: Petros Giannakouris/AP Back to the political crisis in Belgium for a moment where earlier this morning prime minister Bart De Wever tendered his resignation to King Philippe . A statement said Philippe was “withholding his decision” for now.
The Brussels Times reports that “De Wever will visit Philippe again on Friday, when the king will make a final decision on his resignation.”
De Wever’s move came after the five-party coalition he leads could not agree on a budget. If his resignation is accepted, then either another party might be invited to attempt to form a coalition based on the existing parliamentary balance, or new elections may be held.
Prime minister Bart De Wever leaves after a meeting at the Royal Palace. Photograph: Nicolas Maeterlinck/Belga/Shutterstock SuperValu, Ireland’s third-largest supermarket chain, says it’s also had some of its freezer temperatures in-store tampered with, in this second wave of suspected cyber hackings of supermarkets across Europe .
SuperValu said a cyber incident had taken place at 13 of its 233 stores – and that it’s also been forced to throw out chilled and frozen products that have spoiled.
In Estonia , a manufacturer of the affected fridge technology said one its clients had been affected, and the cyber-hackers had gotten into a computer controlling the refrigeration levels and turned the temperature up to 50C. The Selver chain said one of its stores was affected.
As we’ve been reporting, supermarkets across Sweden, Belgium and Luxembourg all experienced this temperature- control meddling overnight.
In Belgium, affected chains include Spar, Carrefour, Delhaize, Intermarche, and in Sweden, ICA, Coop and Axfood.
Employees empty freezers to load shopping carts with frozen goods that have to be thrown away at an ICA supermarket in Sjoebo, Sweden on November 2, 2026 Photograph: Johan Nilsson/TT NEWS AGENCY/AFP/Getty Images Carrefour said 15 of its stores in Belgium had been affected by the hack. The chain was targeted in a mass cyber attack in France last month.
“It’s a cyberattack, there is no other reason,” Carrefour Belgium spokesman Mich Vergauwen told AFP news agency, but noting the “impact is very limited”.
He said 15 stores among 700 in total were affected but not every refrigerator was impacted.

An aerial view of the Iranian shores and the island of Qeshm in the strait of Hormuz. Photograph: Nicolas Economou/Reuters
US reportedly strikes Iran’s Qeshm Island as Vance voices optimism about a deal
Iranian state media reported the sound of explosions on the island in the strait of Hormuz, coming on the eve of crucial US midterms
The ⁠US launched limited strikes on ​Iran’s Qeshm Island late on Monday, ⁠according to reports in US media, hours after US vice-president JD Vance said he was optimistic diplomatic efforts to end the war were moving in the right direction.
The strikes were reported as being “defensive”, and not thought to be a signal of a return to full hostilities, but came on the eve of crucial midterm elections in which Donald Trump’s Republican party is expected to be punished by voters for the cascading effect the war has had on the US cost of living.
When asked earlier on Monday whether he had considered resuming strikes on Iran after Tuesday’s midterm elections, Trump replied “no”.
Oil price falls amid hope of a breakthrough to end Iran war
Several explosions were ⁠heard ⁠on Qeshm ​Island on Monday evening, according to Iranian state media, with local outlets describing their cause as unclear. The strikes – first reported by the Wall Street Journal (WSJ) – targeted surface to air missiles being used against US assets, according to Reuters and the Associated Press.
US Central ‌Command did ​not immediately ⁠respond to ​a request for ​comment from the Reuters news agency, and the WSJ described the attacks as part of a series of strikes carried out against the country in recent weeks that have not been made public.
The paper said that sources suggested the recent strikes have been carried out on a smaller scale and purposefully kept secret by the Trump administration so as not to signal ‌any intent of resuming the military campaign against Iran.
The US has targeted Qeshm Island on multiple occasions throughout the war. Positioned in the mouth of the strait of Hormuz, the island has been used in the past to launch attacks on shipping in the waterway.
Despite attacks having ceased in recent weeks, Iran has continued to enforce its closure of the strait by targeting oil tankers, shipping containers and other vessels attempting to transit the waterway.
If confirmed, the attack would mark the first publicly known strike by the US on Iran in weeks . On Monday Vance said that he and Trump were optimistic about securing a deal with Iran , after Tehran revealed indirect negotiations with Washington.
“The president and I both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement,” Vance told reporters. “We’ve certainly made some progress. We’ll see if we can make some more.”
Speaking to Fox News hours before the polls opened in the US on Tuesday, Trump continued to play down the significance of the conflict and its effects on the US economy.
“There’s no war raging. It could happen if they don’t make a deal, but they want to make a deal very badly and there’s a very good chance we make a deal.”
Speaking from Washington in his closing message of the midterms campaign, Trump hailed a sharp drop in oil prices that came as his administration touted a renewed diplomatic efforts being made to end the war. Rising petrol prices have caused by the war have become a signature issue of the midterm elections, with polls showing voters likely to punish Republicans for the effect on the cost of living.

Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia – Across the Asia-Pacific region, governments and businesses reeling from the energy shock of the United States and Israel’s war on Iran are watching Tuesday’s US midterm elections closely.
Many want to see “enormous changes” during the rest of President Donald Trump’s term, analysts say, from the war on Iran to his policies on trade and tariffs. But few expect that to happen, even with the Democrats poised to take the House of Representatives, and potentially the Senate, from Trump’s Republican Party.

“Of course, everybody is watching,” said Steven Okun, a trade specialist and the chief executive of APAC Advisors, a Singapore-based consulting firm. “It’s great political theatre.”
Outside the Middle East, no region has been hit harder by the war on Iran than the Asia-Pacific. Before the start of the conflict in January, the region took in most of the Gulf oil and gas that passed through the Strait of Hormuz.
When Iran closed the chokepoint in response to the US and Israel’s strikes, much of the region was left facing shortages .
The Philippines, which relies on the Gulf for more than 90 percent of its crude oil imports, has been under a national energy emergency since March. Soaring fuel costs have drained the foreign exchange reserves of the region’s poorest economies – Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar and East Timor, according to the Institute of Southeast Asian Studies (ISEAS)-Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore. Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and Vietnam have also spent heavily on fuel subsidies to shield consumers, it said.
Public opinion in the Asia-Pacific region remains firmly opposed to the war, but Okun said a Democratic-controlled US Congress was unlikely to force Trump to end the eight-month conflict.
“With Iran, I don’t see [a Democrat-controlled Congress] having much change at all, other than the fact that the war will be investigated and there will be oversight hearings,” Okun told Al Jazeera. “We might even see an impeachment of the secretary of defence, but it doesn’t change the overall impact of the war.”
Under the US Constitution, Congress holds the power to formally declare war, but Trump has claimed the attacks on Iran were in self-defence and has so far ignored congressional resolutions directing him to withdraw US forces from hostilities. If a Democrat-controlled Congress passes legislation restricting military operations or cutting funding for them, Trump can veto it. Overriding a veto requires a two-thirds majority in both chambers, which Democrats are almost certain to fall short of.
On trade and tariffs, too, analysts see little room for Congress to rein in Trump.
The US president rattled global markets last year when he imposed “reciprocal” tariffs of 10 percent to 50 percent on some 90 countries, with the aim of shrinking the US trade deficit. Asia was again hit harder than most. Cambodia faced a 49 percent tariff and Laos 48 percent. Vietnam was slapped with 46 percent and Myanmar 45 percent.
After the Supreme Court struck down those tariffs in February, the Trump administration turned to other tools . In July, it imposed tariffs of 10 percent and 12.5 percent on goods from 60 trading partners, accusing them of failing to stop imports made with forced labour . In Asia, the list includes China, Japan, South Korea and seven Southeast Asian nations – Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
“In some ways, the new Congress is not going to matter to the Asia Pacific because it’s not going to affect trade policy,” Okun said. “Congress cannot change that … Tariffs don’t change. The war doesn’t change.”
Stephen Olson, a visiting fellow at the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute, argued in a recent essay that a “strong rebuke of ‘Trumpism’” at the polls could embolden a pro-free-trade wing of the Republican Party that has been “intimidated into standing down during the Trump presidency”.
That, Olson wrote, offers “a glimmer of hope” for Southeast Asian countries that depend on the US market. A Democratic-controlled Congress, he said, could also push for carve-outs and exceptions that would give the region’s exporters “a modicum of relief”. But any deeper shift in US trade policy, he added, will have to wait for the 2028 presidential election.
Joshua Kurlantzick, a senior fellow for Southeast Asia and South Asia at the Council on Foreign Relations, said the region’s wish list goes beyond trade to security.
“I think nearly all of Asia would like to see enormous changes, across many domains, during the rest of Trump’s term,” he told Al Jazeera. “But I think much of the region believes this will not happen.”
Besides “more stability” in trade and tariff policy, Asia-Pacific countries “would like to feel more stable in security guarantees from the US,” he said. They would also like a “more clear, obvious US presence” in the South China Sea , where China’s claims overlap with those of five Southeast Asian nations, and in the Taiwan Strait , which separates China from Taiwan , the self-governed island Beijing claims as its territory.
Businesses will also be watching whether a major Republican loss leads to “greater GOP willingness in Congress to stand up to Trump, along with Democrats, on issues important to companies in Asia,” Kurlantzick said, including tariffs, trade policy, arms sales and “overall economic unpredictability”.
One area where analysts do expect some change is US policy on Chinese technology.
The new Congress, whichever party controls it, will pass tougher restrictions on China, said Okun at APAC Advisors.
These include the Remote Access Security Act, which would extend export controls to remote access of US goods, software or technology and the Chip Security Act, which would require companies to verify that advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips remain in authorised locations, to prevent diversion to foreign adversaries. It also includes the Multilateral Alignment of Technology Controls on Hardware Act, known as the MATCH Act, which would press allies to bring their controls on chipmaking equipment in line with Washington’s, to keep advanced chipmaking technology out of China’s hands.
“The next Congress is going to pass them regardless of midterms because both parties agree on them,” Okun said. “The person who is least restrictive now on China is the US president,” he added, referring to Trump’s courting of China’s President Xi Jinping.
The two men have met twice this year as ties have warmed after a bitter and costly trade war last year. To preserve the fragile trade truce, Trump has also held off approving a $14bn package of arms sales to Taiwan, which would be the largest ever for Taipei.
Some analysts meanwhile worry that a lame-duck Trump, hemmed in at home by a Democratic Congress, could turn more forcefully to foreign policy.
“We should not be surprised by continued erratic foreign policy,” said James Guild, an assistant professor at the Indonesian International Islamic University.
“The Democrats have a poor record of effectively opposing and holding Trump accountable using conventional tools of congressional oversight,” Guild said. “We will have to wait and see if they rise to the moment this time.”

The Philippines, which relies on the Gulf for more than 90 percent of its crude oil imports, has been under a national energy emergency since March. Soaring fuel costs have drained the foreign exchange reserves of the region’s poorest economies – Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar and East Timor, according to the Institute of Southeast Asian Studies (ISEAS)-Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore. Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and Vietnam have also spent heavily on fuel subsidies to shield consumers, it said.
Public opinion in the Asia-Pacific region remains firmly opposed to the war, but Okun said a Democratic-controlled US Congress was unlikely to force Trump to end the eight-month conflict.
“With Iran, I don’t see [a Democrat-controlled Congress] having much change at all, other than the fact that the war will be investigated and there will be oversight hearings,” Okun told Al Jazeera. “We might even see an impeachment of the secretary of defence, but it doesn’t change the overall impact of the war.”
Under the US Constitution, Congress holds the power to formally declare war, but Trump has claimed the attacks on Iran were in self-defence and has so far ignored congressional resolutions directing him to withdraw US forces from hostilities. If a Democrat-controlled Congress passes legislation restricting military operations or cutting funding for them, Trump can veto it. Overriding a veto requires a two-thirds majority in both chambers, which Democrats are almost certain to fall short of.
On trade and tariffs, too, analysts see little room for Congress to rein in Trump.
The US president rattled global markets last year when he imposed “reciprocal” tariffs of 10 percent to 50 percent on some 90 countries, with the aim of shrinking the US trade deficit. Asia was again hit harder than most. Cambodia faced a 49 percent tariff and Laos 48 percent. Vietnam was slapped with 46 percent and Myanmar 45 percent.
After the Supreme Court struck down those tariffs in February, the Trump administration turned to other tools . In July, it imposed tariffs of 10 percent and 12.5 percent on goods from 60 trading partners, accusing them of failing to stop imports made with forced labour . In Asia, the list includes China, Japan, South Korea and seven Southeast Asian nations – Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
“In some ways, the new Congress is not going to matter to the Asia Pacific because it’s not going to affect trade policy,” Okun said. “Congress cannot change that … Tariffs don’t change. The war doesn’t change.”
Stephen Olson, a visiting fellow at the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute, argued in a recent essay that a “strong rebuke of ‘Trumpism’” at the polls could embolden a pro-free-trade wing of the Republican Party that has been “intimidated into standing down during the Trump presidency”.
That, Olson wrote, offers “a glimmer of hope” for Southeast Asian countries that depend on the US market. A Democratic-controlled Congress, he said, could also push for carve-outs and exceptions that would give the region’s exporters “a modicum of relief”. But any deeper shift in US trade policy, he added, will have to wait for the 2028 presidential election.
Joshua Kurlantzick, a senior fellow for Southeast Asia and South Asia at the Council on Foreign Relations, said the region’s wish list goes beyond trade to security.
“I think nearly all of Asia would like to see enormous changes, across many domains, during the rest of Trump’s term,” he told Al Jazeera. “But I think much of the region believes this will not happen.”
Besides “more stability” in trade and tariff policy, Asia-Pacific countries “would like to feel more stable in security guarantees from the US,” he said. They would also like a “more clear, obvious US presence” in the South China Sea , where China’s claims overlap with those of five Southeast Asian nations, and in the Taiwan Strait , which separates China from Taiwan , the self-governed island Beijing claims as its territory.
Businesses will also be watching whether a major Republican loss leads to “greater GOP willingness in Congress to stand up to Trump, along with Democrats, on issues important to companies in Asia,” Kurlantzick said, including tariffs, trade policy, arms sales and “overall economic unpredictability”.
One area where analysts do expect some change is US policy on Chinese technology.
The new Congress, whichever party controls it, will pass tougher restrictions on China, said Okun at APAC Advisors.
These include the Remote Access Security Act, which would extend export controls to remote access of US goods, software or technology and the Chip Security Act, which would require companies to verify that advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips remain in authorised locations, to prevent diversion to foreign adversaries. It also includes the Multilateral Alignment of Technology Controls on Hardware Act, known as the MATCH Act, which would press allies to bring their controls on chipmaking equipment in line with Washington’s, to keep advanced chipmaking technology out of China’s hands.
“The next Congress is going to pass them regardless of midterms because both parties agree on them,” Okun said. “The person who is least restrictive now on China is the US president,” he added, referring to Trump’s courting of China’s President Xi Jinping.
The two men have met twice this year as ties have warmed after a bitter and costly trade war last year. To preserve the fragile trade truce, Trump has also held off approving a $14bn package of arms sales to Taiwan, which would be the largest ever for Taipei.
Some analysts meanwhile worry that a lame-duck Trump, hemmed in at home by a Democratic Congress, could turn more forcefully to foreign policy.
“We should not be surprised by continued erratic foreign policy,” said James Guild, an assistant professor at the Indonesian International Islamic University.
“The Democrats have a poor record of effectively opposing and holding Trump accountable using conventional tools of congressional oversight,” Guild said. “We will have to wait and see if they rise to the moment this time.”

items.summary: Oil price falls amid hope of a breakthrough to end Iran war  The Guardian
items.content:
The strait of Hormuz shipping lane has been largely closed since the US and Israel attacked Iran earlier this year. Photograph: Reuters
The strait of Hormuz shipping lane has been largely closed since the US and Israel attacked Iran earlier this year. Photograph: Reuters
Oil price falls amid hope of a breakthrough to end Iran war
Brent crude drops by more than 6% to $105.55 a barrel, the lowest level in more than two weeks
The oil price has fallen to its lowest level in more two weeks amid new hopes of a breakthrough to end the Iran war.
Brent crude, the international benchmark, dropped by more than 6.5% to as low as $105.55 a barrel on Monday, the lowest since 16 October, sending shares in airline companies higher and pushing down government borrowing costs.
Oil prices fell after Tehran revealed that contacts between Iran and the US to end their eight-month war were continuing.
“Consultations through mediators are very ⁠intensive. We have presented our conditions and ⁠proposals and everything depends on the political ​rationality of Washington,” the Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said, according to the state media outlet IRNA.
Over the weekend, Qatari officials tried to negotiate the release of more than $6bn (£4.5bn) in Iranian assets , so that Tehran might allow the strait of Hormuz to reopen.
On Monday, US vice-president JD Vance reported that there had been “a number of good conversations with the Iranians” and that he was feeling good about the prospects of a “negotiated settlement”.
Vance sent a letter to Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, last week but the White House has offered few details about the contents of that correspondence.
Donald Trump had earlier taken a belligerent tone, telling voters in Iowa on Sunday that Iran would receive “the hammer” unless there was progress.
“The only reason why I’m not finished with Iran is I want to be nice. I want to try and save all those lives if I can ... But at some point we’re going to have to give them the hammer,” he said during a campaign rally in the run-up to the US midterm elections.
But investors were cheered by reports on Monday that Iran’s supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, had granted “powers” to his government in its talks with the US seeking to end the Middle East war.
Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said: “The news is manna from heaven for stock markets, which have felt increasingly pressured by oil’s rise, but of course there is still a risk that Trump will try one last throw of the iron dice after the midterms.”
The drop in the oil price sparked hopes of a break in the inflationary pressures gripping the global economy. Government borrowing costs dropped, with the yield – or interest rate – on 10-year UK bonds down 10 basis points, or 0.1 of a percentage point, to the lowest since 22 September.
Shares in British Airways’ parent company, IAG, rose by 4.2% in London, while United Airlines jumped 7% in New York.

items.title: Thousands of European troops to rehearse Ukraine deployment in event of peace
items.summary: Western officials stress that any force sent to Ukraine would not take part in any offensive operations.
items.content:
Image caption, A British paratrooper takes part in a previous Nato training exercise less than 50km (31 miles) from the Russian border in Finland
Britain and France are to lead a military exercise to test a multinational force's ability to deploy to Ukraine, if there is a peace deal.
Nearly 3,000 military personnel from 12 European nations will take part in the rehearsal in neighbouring Poland this month.
Plans for a reassurance force for Ukraine were set out last year as one of the long-term security guarantees being proposed by European nations.
But there are still more questions than answers as to how such a military force might work in practice. Western officials stress that any force sent to Ukraine would not take part in offensive operations or be involved in peacekeeping or ceasefire monitoring missions.
Nor would they be operating under the command of Nato or on the front line.
Officials say their presence would be to provide reassurance to Ukraine and to help rebuild its armed forces.
The US has been involved in discussions, but is not contributing to the mission.
Russia has already voiced opposition to foreign troops being stationed in Ukraine and, last year, President Vladimir Putin said they would be "legitimate targets".
Western officials have declined to spell out the rules of engagement if any international troops were to be attacked in Ukraine. Though they say the force would be able to defend itself.
UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the exercise showed Britain, France and their allies were stepping up preparation for the day when peace came to Ukraine.
He said: "This is not a hypothetical plan, it's a real force, ready to help Ukraine once the fighting stops."
Lt Gen Tom Bateman, the UK commander of the Multi National Force â Ukraine (MNF-U), said the exercise represented an important step in translating political commitments into credible military readiness.
He said it was a "real, capable, readily deployable force that represented a serious commitment from Coalition of the Willing nations to Ukraine's long-term stability and security".
Image caption, Ukrainian troops take part in urban warfare training at a military base in England in 2023
Exercise Koalicja - which takes place from 9-22 November - will be a rehearsal of how to move, protect and supply a force in Ukraine. It will also be a test of their command and control to ensure troops from different countries can work together.
Some 2,800 military personnel will take part across land, sea and air, with the UK contribution including 300 troops and a pair of RAF Typhoons.
Fighter jets will simulate how they would reassure commercial aircraft once Ukraine's skies can be reopened.
Turkey has agreed to lead the maritime mission, with the eventual goal to clear mines and allow the resumption of trade in the Black Sea.
As well as the UK, troops will come from France, Belgium, Estonia, France, Germany, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Poland, Spain, Sweden, and Turkey.
However, Western officials could not comment on the final make-up and shape of the force that could be deployed to Ukraine if the fighting stops.
In the past, military experts have suggested that Western nations might have to send tens of thousands of troops to Ukraine to guarantee its security.
Officials acknowledge that the countries' commitment and contributions will depend on the circumstances of a cessation of hostilities and individual nations' political decisions.
It is also unclear what training role Western forces could provide to battle hardened Ukraine.
Ukrainian soldiers are already in high demand training Nato forces - passing on their expertise in drone warfare.
Above all, Russia has shown no sign of wanting to end its war.

items.title: Shop freezers in seven European countries hit by cyber-attack
items.summary: The temperature of freezers in several shops across Europe reportedly rose to as high as 50C.
items.content:
Figure caption, 'All this food is now useless': Piles of rubbish after shop freezers hit by cyber-attack
Dozens of supermarkets across seven European countries have been hit by a cyber-attack affecting their refrigerators and freezers.
Around 40 Delhaize supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected, while a smaller number of shops were hit in Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.
Sabcobel, a Belgian company that manufactures some of the affected refrigerators, said the units' evaporators were switched to defrost mode, causing them to warm up, in what is believed to be the same method used in last month's incident that hit hundreds of French supermarkets.
Millions of euros worth of food had to be thrown away in October, local media reported at the time.
Image source, TT NEWS AGENCY / AFP via Getty Images
Image caption, Freezers have had to be emptied at several ICA grocery stores in Sweden after the cyber-attack
Stephan Moelans, the CEO of Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize's systems, on Monday told the Belga news agency that the incident was a cyber-attack and that the company had been "working all night and morning to disconnect the affected units from the network".
He said since the French attack in early October, the company had been working to "protect our customers fridges against this vulnerability" but that the units needed physical modifications, not just software updates.
Most supermarkets across Europe are linked to the internet, and maintenance and troubleshooting can be done remotely.
"The simplest solution is to manage the fridges over a secure internet connection. Most of our customers switched to that after the attack in France," Moelans added.
The temperature of freezers in several shops across Europe reportedly rose to as high as 50C (122F).
It is unclear who is behind the latest apparent attack.
In the US, authorities are investigating what caused refrigeration malfunctions at a number of American military bases in August and working together with French officials to examine whether the incidents could be linked.
Both Belgium and Sweden's national cyber-security agencies said they were monitoring the incident.
The UK's National Cyber Security Centre said it was working with international partners and industry to "fully understand details of an incident". No incidents have been reported in the UK.
In Flanders, northern Belgium, a Delhaize branch in Hoeilaart told news website Het Laatste Nieuws it had lost â¬100,000 (Â£83,500) worth of produce.
The manager said that estimate did not even take into account further losses that would result from closing the shop.
Carrefour, a French-owned supermarket, said the incident had only affected 15 of its Belgian stores, adding that measures had been taken immediately to ensure all shops remained open.
A spokesperson for Colruyt Group, which operates Spar stores in Belgium under a franchise system, told Reuters news agency five shops had their fridge systems attacked.
Sweden's budget furniture retailer Ikea said refrigeration systems of its store in the western Belgian city of Mons were affected, with a spokesman quoted by Reuters as saying "we cannot rule out that additional locations may be affected".
Image caption, An employee at an ICA supermarket in Sweden's capital Stockholm was pictured throwing away bags of spoiled food
A spokesperson for ICA confirmed the incident had affected a "small number of ICA stores operating outside ICA's central network".
"ICA is currently supporting the affected stores in managing the situation," they said.
One of the ICA branches located in SjÃ¶bo, southern Sweden, wrote on social media: "Our refrigerators and freezers have been hacked overnight and they have set the temperature to 50 degrees."
The store was closed earlier but has now reopened to customers.
Seven out of the 800 Coop stores in Sweden were also affected but the "situation is currently contained and under control", the company told the BBC.
In neighbouring Finland, refrigerator malfunctions were detected in some K-stores.
The owner of the supermarket chain Kesko was quoted by Finland's Helsingin Sanomat newspaper as saying its security experts were investigating what caused the problem.
The attack is also affecting shops in Ireland, the Netherlands and Estonia.
In Ireland, it impacted 13 SuperValu supermarkets. A spokesman for the owner of the chain, Musgrave Group, confirmed to The Irish Times that a "cyber incident" affected its refrigeration systems, but added that the impact was limited to a "specific model" of refrigerator.
A spokesperson for Danish manufacturer Danfoss told Dutch public radio channel NOS that the freezing and cooling systems of at least 17 companies in the Netherlands were attacked overnight, affecting butcher shops and small neighbourhood stores.
A Selver supermarket in Estonia was also affected and there are reports of other affected companies in the country, according to ERR.

Here's How Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway Stock Did in Every S&P 500 Down Year Since 2000
Counting dividends, the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) has been down in six calendar years since 2000. Berkshire Hathaway (NYSE:BRKA)(NYSE:BRKB) stock beat the index in all of them.
The record is from Berkshire's own annual letter, which has a table comparing the yearly change in its per-share market value to the S&P 500 's return, including dividends.
Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »
In 2000, Berkshire's stock rose 26.6% but the index slid 9.1%. It added 6.5% in 2001 versus an 11.9% decline, and it dipped just 3.8% in 2002, as the index shed 22.1%. In 2008, the stock fell 31.8%, a little less than the index's 37% drop. And in 2018 and 2022, Berkshire climbed 2.8% and 4% but the index fell 4.4% and 18.1%.
So, Berkshire made money in four of those six years. On a simple average, the stock gained less than 1% a year over all six, while the index dropped around 17%.
Of course, the definition matters here. A down year in this case follows the table's S&P column, which counts dividends. Berkshire hasn't paid a dividend since 1967, so its column is just the change in the stock's market value.
On price alone, two more years would make the list. The index ended 2011 a fraction of a point down and dropped 0.7% in 2015. And Berkshire's shares slid both years, by 4.7% and 12.5%, so the streak arguably depends on where the line gets drawn.
Warren Buffett wrote about keeping Berkshire liquid for decades, and he stuck to it in 2008, the worst of those six years for the market. That year, Berkshire put $14.5 billion into high-yielding fixed-income securities from three companies, getting an equity stake in each deal as a bonus. To pay for them, Buffett trimmed some stock holdings he would've preferred to keep.
In his 2008 letter to shareholders, he said that he'd pledged to always run Berkshire "with more than ample cash."
"We never want to count on the kindness of strangers in order to meet tomorrow's obligations," Buffett wrote.
But that pledge was about the company, not the share price. Berkshire's stock still lost 31.8% in 2008. And the calendar-year number hides the worst of it. In his 2017 letter, Buffett listed the stock's largest drops, including a 50.7% slide in the Class A shares between Sept. 19, 2008, and March 5, 2009.
He never said the stock was immune, either. In his 2014 letter, Buffett noted that Berkshire's shares had fallen around 50% from a peak three times since 1965.
"Someday, something close to this kind of drop will happen again, and no one knows when," he wrote.
I'd say the record's best run also owes something to where the stock started. According to the same 2017 letter, Berkshire's Class A shares slid 48.9% between June 1998 and March 2000, bottoming at $41,300. That was only about 9% over the $37,987 in book value per share Berkshire reported for the end of 1999 (book value is what's left after subtracting a company's liabilities from its assets).
Notably, Berkshire's edge was narrowest in 2008, at about 5 percentage points, the year the market's drop was largest. In the other five down years, the margin ranged from around 7 points in 2018 to about 36 points in 2000.
Berkshire's Class B shares closed at around $542 on Oct. 29, under 2% off their 52-week high of $549.96. With book value of around $348 per Class B share at the end of June, the stock trades at about 1.6 times book value -- well over the roughly 1.1 times book value it hit in March 2000.
The cash, of course, is still there. Greg Abel, Berkshire's CEO since January, described a "fortress-like balance sheet" in his first annual letter. And Berkshire had around $365 billion in cash and Treasury bills at the end of June, or about 31% of its market value at the Oct. 29 close. Some of that money is needed to back Berkshire's insurance business, Abel said.
Still, can investors count on Berkshire in the next down year? I think the record makes a decent case that the stock could hold up better than the index again. But it doesn't promise a gain, and the shares aren't starting from anywhere near their March 2000 valuation.
For me, that still makes Berkshire worth owning as a steadier part of a portfolio. I'd just expect its edge in the next down year to be narrower than it was in 2000.

items.content:
US Stock Futures Rise Ahead of Apple Earnings as Binance Hack, Oil Prices and Midterm Elections Take Focus: Dow Jones, S&P, Nasdaq, Wall Street
Wall Street bull ©Shutterstock US stock futures moved higher on Monday, pointing to a potential recovery on Wall Street following October's technology-led selloff, as investors prepared for major corporate earnings, the US midterm elections and further developments in the Middle East.
Apple's upcoming financial results are attracting particular attention, with new Chief Executive John Ternus preparing to lead his first earnings conference call. Meanwhile, a reported multibillion-dollar security breach at cryptocurrency exchange Binance has raised concerns about digital asset security.
Oil prices also declined sharply as investors assessed the possibility of diplomatic progress in the conflict involving the United States, Israel and Iran.
Apple Earnings to Test Growth Outlook Under New CEO
Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) is scheduled to report earnings on Monday, with investors focusing on the company's growth prospects, artificial intelligence strategy and the potential impact of higher component costs.
John Ternus, who succeeded Tim Cook as chief executive in September, will host his first earnings conference call in the role.
His appointment followed the introduction of several products, including Apple's first foldable iPhone, a smart home hub and its first touchscreen laptops. Shipments of these devices began during the company's current fiscal first quarter.
Investors will examine Apple's guidance for the important holiday shopping period, alongside management's plans for artificial intelligence and the updated Siri platform.
Rising memory chip prices are another area of concern, with analysts expecting higher production costs to affect profitability. Profit growth could slow to its weakest pace in six quarters.
Apple also regained its position as the world's most valuable publicly traded company on Friday, overtaking Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA).
Despite a 1.2% decline in Apple's share price, its market capitalisation stood at $5.03 trillion at the close. Nvidia's valuation fell to $4.93 trillion after its shares dropped 4.2%.
The shift came as investors reassessed the scale of artificial intelligence infrastructure spending and the time required for those investments to generate returns.
Binance Faces $3.64 Billion in Withdrawals Following Reported Hack
Cryptocurrency exchange Binance experienced customer withdrawals totalling $3.64 billion after resuming operations following a major security breach reportedly linked to North Korea.
The withdrawals represented approximately 2.1% of the platform's assets.
The incident reportedly involved the theft of $6.3 billion from the exchange during the previous week, raising questions about security and confidence across the cryptocurrency industry.
Binance said withdrawal activity was stabilising following an initial surge and reported that customer deposits remained substantial.
As of 28 October, the exchange reported total assets under management of $171 billion and approximately 335 million registered users worldwide.
Cryptocurrency prices showed signs of stabilisation following recent losses.
Bitcoin (COIN:BTCUSD) recovered above $78,000 on Monday after reaching a six-week low on Friday.
Ether (COIN:ETHUSD) also rebounded modestly to approximately $2,287, following a decline to its lowest level in two months.
Market participants remain attentive to customer flows and the potential consequences of the reported breach for confidence in digital asset platforms.
Wall Street Futures Advance Following October Technology Selloff
US stock index futures rose in early Monday trading, suggesting a stronger opening following the previous month's weakness in technology shares.
By 03:50 ET, S&P 500 futures had gained 0.46% to 7,614 points, while Nasdaq 100 futures advanced 0.75% to 28,753 points. Dow Jones futures increased 0.28% to 52,075 points.
Technology stocks also recovered across Asian markets, helping support sentiment towards US equity futures.
Investors are preparing for another active earnings week, with Apple due to publish results on Monday and Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) scheduled to report on Tuesday.
Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ:PLTR) and Berkshire Hathaway are also expected to release financial results on Monday.
The announcements will provide further information about corporate profitability, technology spending and the outlook for major US businesses.
Oil Prices Fall More Than 3% Amid Renewed Diplomatic Expectations
Crude oil prices declined sharply on Monday as investors assessed prospects for diplomatic progress in the conflict involving the United States, Israel and Iran.
Brent crude futures for January delivery fell 3.3% to $109.70 per barrel by 00:27 ET, while US West Texas Intermediate futures dropped 3.5% to $100.48 per barrel.
The decline followed a strong October rally, during which both benchmarks gained nearly 15%.
The absence of a major escalation over the weekend encouraged some traders to take profits after recent price increases.
According to a report by Axios, President Donald Trump told Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during a Saturday telephone conversation that he preferred to allow more time for diplomacy before deciding whether to resume military operations.
The report also indicated that Netanyahu favoured renewed US strikes shortly after the midterm elections.
Lower crude prices could help reduce energy-related inflation pressures for businesses and consumers.
However, oil prices remain elevated following October's gains, leaving markets sensitive to further developments in the conflict and potential supply disruptions.
US Midterm Elections Bring Fiscal and Regulatory Policy Into Focus
The US midterm elections scheduled for Tuesday represent another important event for financial markets, with the results set to determine the composition of Congress during the second half of President Donald Trump's term.
All 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 Senate seats are being contested.
The elections take place against a backdrop of concerns about elevated gasoline prices and the prolonged conflict with Iran.
A recent Reuters/Ipsos survey placed Trump's approval rating at 31%, the lowest level recorded in that poll.
The composition of the next Congress could influence the administration's ability to advance legislation covering fiscal policy, trade, taxation and regulation.
If Democrats secure control of both chambers, the administration could face greater legislative obstacles. A divided Congress could also increase reliance on executive actions in areas where legislation proves difficult.
For investors, the election results may affect expectations for government spending, business regulation and the broader economic policy environment.
Wall Street enters the new trading week with several important developments influencing investor sentiment.
Apple's earnings and other major corporate results will provide fresh evidence about technology demand, profitability and artificial intelligence investment.
At the same time, the reported Binance security breach has increased scrutiny of cryptocurrency markets, while declining oil prices have offered some relief from inflation concerns.
The US midterm elections and developments in the Iran conflict remain additional sources of uncertainty, with potential implications for fiscal policy, energy markets and broader financial conditions.

items.content:
Share How US oil firms profit $130bn from Iran war as household bills surge on social media
ExxonMobil and Chevron, the biggest US oil companies, on Friday reported profits from almost $10bn to more than $15bn [File: Dado Ruvic/Reuters]
United States oil companies have earned more than $130bn in profits during the war on Iran, even as consumers pay much higher prices for key commodities, amid fears that US President Donald Trump may renew fighting after midterm elections .
The estimate, released by The New York Times, is a conservative evaluation based on the performance of 51 large US oil and gas companies in the six months from April through September. By contrast, in the same period in 2025 – when the prices of oil were lower prior to the launch of the US-Israel war on Iran – they collectively earned less than $47bn.

list 2 of 3 Iran and US explore diplomacy amid rising threats of war
list 3 of 3 More than 50 million votes cast in US midterm elections: What does it mean?
But the gains come as burgeoning living costs are crushing consumers. Americans have spent an extra $150bn on petrol and diesel since the war on Iran began on February 28, according to an analysis by Brown University ’s Climate Solutions Lab, which amounts to more than $1,150 per household.
The disparity has fuelled a political debate over who gains and who pays the price for the war. Responding to Trump, Democratic Representative Jim McGovern wrote on X: “We’re not making a ‘freaking fortune,’ we’re PAYING a ‘freaking fortune’.”
Naser al-Tamimi, a fellow at the Institute for International Political Studies (ISPI) in Milan, Italy, said US energy companies have benefitted from the war in different ways. “Crude producers gain from higher oil prices, while refiners capture exceptional margins as diesel and other fuel supplies tighten,” he said.
Additionally, “damage to Middle Eastern and Russian refineries, disrupted Strait of Hormuz shipments , and sanctions-related trade frictions have intensified shortages”, while “relatively secure US facilities and access to discounted crude strengthen these gains”.
ExxonMobil and Chevron, the biggest US oil companies, on Friday reported profits of between $10bn and $15bn. While the gains are considerable, The New York Times found they generally remained below 2022 levels, when Russia’s invasion of Ukraine caused oil prices to soar to roughly $100 a barrel and raised natural gas prices, compared with the current average of $90 from April through September.
American refining companies also reaped greater profits as global fuel supplies tightened and inventories depleted due to heavy damage to infrastructure in the Middle East and Russia. Valero Energy’s third-quarter profit increased more than sixfold, reaching $6.83bn. Phillips 66 announced its highest quarterly profit on record, with net income jumping to $5.62bn from $133m a year earlier.
Geoffrey Miller, geopolitical analyst and editor of the Gulf States Insights newsletter, said the US-Israel war with Iran “created the largest supply-side shock to global oil and refined products markets in years”.
Miller added that the war “created a risk premium that US-based operators are structurally well placed to monetise”. By contrast, Gulf producers were “hit hard by both higher costs and risks, along with physical damage, which makes their ability to benefit from the higher prices much more difficult”.
Tehran retaliated against the US-Israeli attack by launching missiles and drones at the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC). The Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED), a US-registered independent conflict monitor, found Iran and Iran-backed groups in the region have carried out at least 172 attacks on nonmilitary infrastructure across the six GCC member states. Despite claims by Iranian officials that they were targeting US military facilities, they also hit energy infrastructure.
Iran also effectively blocked passage of most vessels through the Strait of Hormuz. In retaliation, the US imposed a naval blockade on Iranian oil and gas – the tit-for-tat steps raising the risks of transporting energy out of the crucial passageway.
Analysts warned of continued volatility until a durable political settlement between the US and Iran is reached. Oil prices dropped briefly in the summer after a memorandum of understanding was signed in June, but prices quickly soared again when talks broke down.
A more recent escalation in fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis has further compounded the crisis: the Bab al-Mandeb strait that connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden, which Saudi Arabia uses to export oil, is now also a theatre of war.
“In the short term, windfall profits will only strengthen oil company balance sheets and shareholder returns,” Miller said. “However, the big profits come with a major caveat. That’s because over the longer term, high oil prices risk harming economic growth prospects and could even contribute towards the outbreak of a recession, which would in turn be likely to lead to reduced demand for oil” and accelerate the transition to renewable energy.
Florence Schmit, senior energy strategist at Rabobank’s global economics and markets team in London, said it was likely that the prices of key energy products would remain high given the uncertainty about the duration of the war in Iran.
“Prices in all markets that have an exposure to this global supply shock – which includes the US – will face high prices also next year, and consumers will continue to feel this price pressure unless governments step in,” Schmit told Al Jazeera.
The US-led war on Iran has raised costs for oil, transport fuels, gas, electricity and food. According to the World Bank Group’s latest Commodity Markets Outlook, commodity prices are set to rise 23 percent this year, as disrupted grain shipments and the El Nino weather phenomenon also threaten harvests and food affordability.
The United Nations’ Food and Agriculture Organization said on October 2 that world food commodity prices rose a further 1.5 percent in September, after reaching their highest level since late 2022 in August, amid adverse weather and trade disruptions in the Black Sea and Strait of Hormuz.
Trump has sought to blame high global fuel prices on Ukraine and pressured Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to halt strikes on Russian refineries, even as Moscow continued to wage attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure. The US president has argued that a deal with Russia reversing years of sanctions would help lower diesel prices.
In the Gulf, analysts said higher oil prices will benefit exporters that can maintain shipments, but prolonged insecurity will continue to threaten supply reliability and investment.
“Gulf producers face years of reconstruction and pressure to diversify export routes,” ISPI’s al-Tamimi said. “A diplomatic settlement could ease prices, whereas renewed US-Israeli attacks on Iran risk triggering another regional war, further disrupting Hormuz and prolonging shortages.”

San Mateo to expand Delaware basin gas processing capacity under new producer agreements
The project adds about $25 million to San Mateo’s 2026 midstream capital budget, bringing it to $170-190 million, while total processing capacity is expected to exceed 1.3 bcfd.
Assets owned and operated by Matador Resources and its midstream joint venture, San Mateo, include over 1000 miles of pipelines, 20 saltwater disposal wells and processing plants with over 1 bcfd of natural gas processing capacity.
San Mateo Midstream LLC plans to expand natural gas gathering and processing infrastructure in New Mexico's Delaware basin after signing two long-term agreements with a producer.
Matador Resources, Five Point Capital form Delaware basin midstream JV
San Mateo Midstream, a joint venture of Matador Resources Co. (51%) and Five Point Infrastructure LLC (49%), said the agreements are expected to add long-term volumes across its gathering and processing system. With that and anticipated production growth from Matador, the company plans to expand its Marlan natural gas processing complex in Eddy County, NM, with a 300-MMcfd processing train and a new nitrogen rejection unit. The company also expects to construct about 20 miles of natural gas pipeline to connect newly dedicated acreage and a field treating facility for CO 2 removal.
Subject to permitting, procurement, and construction activities, the Marlan expansion is targeted for completion by yearend 2028.
The company said the project will increase its expected 2026 midstream capital expenditures by about $25 million, raising its estimated midstream capital budget for the year to $170-190 million.
The agreements consist of a new long-term fixed-fee gas gathering and processing contract and an extension of an existing gas gathering and processing agreement.
Under the new agreement, San Mateo will gather and treat natural gas from newly dedicated acreage in Lea and Eddy Counties, NM, and process the volumes at the Marlan complex. The agreement includes a large-scale acreage dedication in the northern Delaware basin.
Separately, San Mateo amended an existing gas gathering and processing agreement covering production from Eddy County. Under the extension, gas will continue to be gathered, treated, and processed at the Black River gas processing plant in Eddy County for several years beyond the original contract term. The extension builds on a gas gathering and processing agreement San Mateo announced in October 2018, the company noted.
Upon completion of the Marlan expansion, San Mateo's total natural gas processing capacity will exceed 1.3 bcfd, nearly tripling the 460-MMcfd capacity it had before Matador contributed Pronto Midstream LLC to the venture in December 2024.

Joseph Wm. Foran, Matador founder, chairman, and chief executive officer, and founder of San Mateo, said the agreements build on San Mateo's growth.
"Following the closing of the previously announced Cardinal Midstream acquisition in the third quarter, we completed the connection of the San Mateo and Cardinal systems in southern Eddy County, New Mexico," he said.
"In 2027, San Mateo plans to complete the full system connection with a northern pipeline connecting San Mateo's Lea County gathering infrastructure with the terminus of Cardinal's gathering infrastructure in Eddy County. This connection is expected to allow gas volumes to flow from the Marlan Plant complex in the north to the Pecos River Plant in the south, providing further flexibility for San Mateo and its customers."
He said the newly signed agreements are expected to increase volumes beginning in 2028.

Yardeni Research President Ed Yardeni said Monday that the recent artificial intelligence (AI) sell-off was not a full-blown rout but was “taking some air out of the AI bubble,” which he sees as a positive development.
In an interview with CNBC-TV18, the strategist said he expects semiconductor stocks to rebound, adding that AI is a real technology that will become profitable, although identifying which technology companies will benefit most remains difficult.

Yardeni also expects a year-end rally in U.S. equities but warned that midterm elections and geopolitical uncertainty could create further buying opportunities.
Yardeni said the recent pullback has reduced valuations even as analysts continue raising earnings expectations for AI-related companies.
The market veteran noted that semiconductor stocks trade at a forward price-to-earnings ratio of about 13.5, below the S&P 500's 18.5, adding that cloud revenue growth and substantial order backlogs support his outlook.
In a research note, he said that analysts expect semiconductor industry earnings to grow 114.3% in 2026 and 77.9% in 2027.  The note also showed that Microsoft ( MSFT ), Oracle ( ORCL ), Amazon ( AMZN ) and Alphabet (GOOG, GOOGL) have combined remaining performance obligations of $2.5 trillion.
Yardeni Research identified funding and delivering AI infrastructure as the key challenge to monetizing those commitments. The firm also said memory makers were sold out into 2029, giving them pricing power amid strong AI demand.
Yardeni’s comments come after Friday's sell-off saw Intel ( INTC ) stock plunge 28.6%, SanDisk ( SNDK ) fall 13.5%, and AMD drop 10.9%. However, the analyst said investors were shifting from AI stocks into health care, financials and industrials rather than leaving U.S. equities.
Turning to Tuesday's midterm elections, Yardeni warned that the U.S. stock market could face further volatility amid the possibility of renewed escalation in the war involving Iran.
He said his firm had advised caution since September 15 and suggested investors consider holding back cash for potential buying opportunities following the elections or any further escalation.
Yardeni also warned that greater political division after the elections could make future debt and government shutdown negotiations more difficult, potentially creating risks heading into 2027.
Despite those concerns, he expects a year-end rally in U.S. stocks, typically referred to as a ‘Santa rally’, between Thanksgiving and the end of December.
U.S. stock futures rose early Monday after a losing week on Wall Street, as investors looked ahead to earnings, jobs data and the midterm elections.
S&P 500 futures gained 0.5%, Nasdaq 100 futures climbed 0.80%, and Dow futures advanced 271 points, or 0.52%, following a week of selling in technology stocks amid concerns over artificial intelligence spending.

French pupils resume school blockades as country braces for more protests
Minister warns weeks without lessons are putting exams at risk as unions plan nationwide strike on Thursday
Dozens of high schools across France were blockaded again on Monday as the government braced for another tense week of protests over school conditions and the high cost of living.
The protests come amid warnings that weeks without lessons are putting some pupils’ school year and final exams at risk.
As children returned after the two-week school holiday, students’ unions ignored Emmanuel Macron’s call to end the lycée blockades , which have been running since September and have prompted one of the biggest protest movements and social crises of his presidency.
From early morning in Paris and its suburbs, as well as in cities including Lille, Toulouse and Marseille, schoolchildren demanding more replacement teachers and repairs to buildings barricaded school entrances with wheelie bins. Police officers outside some schools attempted to drag the bins away and made arrests.
Students gather outside a blockaded high school in Paris to protest against a lack of resources. Photograph: Nicolas Garriga/AP University students’ unions were planning additional barricades at faculties on Tuesday. Trade unions have called for a large-scale strike on Thursday, with rail workers, teachers and private-sector employees planning to join demonstrations in cities across France to support schoolchildren’s demands for better conditions and protest against the rising cost of living and low salaries.
Nathanaël Combary from the school students’ union Renouveau Lycéen, who is also a member of Macron’s centrist party Renaissance, said schoolchildren must keep going in their “battle of strength” with the government to push for more funding, better access to higher education and repairs to decrepit schools.
He said measures offered by the government last week to cap some class sizes and review the university applications platform were inadequate. Combary told BFMTV that protests were the only way for schoolchildren to push a government response. He said: “Democratically speaking it’s a bit scandalous that we have to reach this type of situation to be heard but it’s the only solution we have.”
The education minister, Édouard Geffray, said he feared the school year was now “at risk” for many students in their final years who had missed weeks of classes because of the blockades and would be unable to complete coursework or catch up on the curriculum for exams.
He said: “We have pupils who are sitting their baccalauréat at the end of the year who for hundreds of thousands of them have had no classes for four or five weeks if you include holidays, and for whom the school year is now at risk. And that’s something that we can’t allow.”
Geffray said the school blockades were “illegal” and his priority was for children to return to class.
A protester adds a bin to a fire outside the Montebello international high school in Lille. Photograph: François Lo Presti/AFP/Getty Images In Montpellier, the Socialist senator Hussein Bourgi accused the government of “misconduct” and “provocation” after video footage showed a 53-year-old school nurse saying something to police near a school barricade before being forced face-down to the ground, handcuffed and taken into police custody. The local prefect, in charge of police operations, defended the arrest, saying the woman had insulted officers and resisted police.
The education ministry said 41 high schools were blocked across France – around 1% of the nationwide total. Students’ unions put the figure at 150.
Nicolas Bonnet, of the headteachers’ union SNPDEN-UNSA, said: “It’s time for us to return to our job: teaching and supporting pupils.” He warned that coursework, final-year exams and university applications were at risk.
He said he understood why high-school students felt the government had not offered enough to fix problems in schools, but urged more dialogue between the government and pupils.
The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said he would meet school students’ unions again next week.

Stock market after midterm elections: S&P 500 history
The S&P 500 averaged a 13.7% one-year gain after 11 midterm elections since 1980.
After divided-government outcomes, the index averaged a 15% one-year gain, compared to 11.5% under single-party control.
Fed policy, earnings and the AI trade may matter more than the election result.
Markets are sweating it out ahead of the midterm elections, but the event historically heralds strong performance for stocks — regardless of whether it's a red or blue wave, split decision, or status quo in Washington.
The S&P 500 tends to perform well after both midterm and presidential elections. According to a CNBC analysis of S&P 500 returns after elections from 1980 through 2024, the index rose an average of 0.2% after one day and one week, and 1.1% after one month across both presidential and midterm elections.
A year later, the index gained an average of 13.7% after midterms and 13.8% after presidential elections. Returns were positive in 91% of cases. And the S&P 500 was up after all 11 midterms from 1982 through 2022.
Short-term returns were less reliable, particularly after presidential contests, which produced slightly negative average returns after one day and one week.
"There's some anxiousness before these elections," Ryan Detrick, CNBC contributor and chief market strategist at Carson Group, told CNBC. "Once you are through it, it's a big relief and markets tend to do pretty well."
Still, the market usually prefers divided government: one party in charge of the White House and the other holding at least one house of Congress.
Across 10 midterm and five presidential elections that left no single party in charge, the S&P 500 rose an average 15% after one year. One-year returns were positive in 14 out of 15 cases. By comparison, the index gained an average of 11.5% over the year after elections that resulted in single-party control.
"If you have a huge red wave or a big blue wave, markets actually kind of don't like that as much because you have too much spending one way and too much power," Detrick said.
Leaving Democrats in control of Congress with a Republican in the White House — a scenario that may emerge from the elections on Tuesday — was also positive. A CNBC analysis found that after the three midterms (1986, 1990 and 2006) when Democrats controlled both houses and a Republican held the presidency, the S&P 500 averaged a 0.5% decline on the reaction day but was up 3.4% a month later and 10.9% after a year.
Granted, elections may be coincident events to factors that matter far more for market performance.
The S&P 500 plunged 22.1% in the year after the 2000 elections due to the dotcom bust, marking the worst post-election performance since 1980. Conversely, the S&P 500's best post-election year was a 38.3% gain after the 2020 elections, when markets mounted a massive comeback from the COVID-induced selloff.
Investors should bear in mind that Federal Reserve policy and the corporate earnings cycle ultimately matter more than elections, according to Société Générale.
Stocks declined in the aftermath of the 2018 midterms, for instance, when Democrats wrested control of the House during President Donald Trump's first term. More importantly, the Fed tightened monetary policy that year, raising interest rates four times, and the S&P 500 ended the year down 6.2%, though the market was up 11.7% a year after the election.
The big swing factor now is AI and whether declines in tech will continue. As long as the AI wave is still moving and the economy keeps growing, "this bull market is probably still alive and well," Detrick says.
But a Democratic sweep of the House and Senate would almost certainly pressure the AI infrastructure buildout and could lead to more retrenchment.
The bond market is also skittish with yields rising globally and a mini debt crisis in France. And the war with Iran could get worse post-election if President Trump follows through on threats of more strikes or Iran escalates.
"Seasonality isn't destiny, and worries around Iran, AI and France won't mysteriously vanish," said Jim Reid, Deutsche Bank's global head of macro and thematic research, in a note.
If history is any guide, we could see a Santa rally and S&P 500 gains after the midterms. But this is still an AI-driven market, with geopolitics, the Fed, and bond market very much in charge.
