items.title: Hackers send fake nuclear threat alert to Ukraine emergency app - The Guardian
items.summary: Hackers send fake nuclear threat alert to Ukraine emergency app  The Guardian
items.content:
Many residents of Kyiv ignored the alerts, which were sent at about 11pm on Sunday. Photograph: Maxym Marusenko/NurPhoto/Shutterstock
Many residents of Kyiv ignored the alerts, which were sent at about 11pm on Sunday. Photograph: Maxym Marusenko/NurPhoto/Shutterstock
Hackers send fake nuclear threat alert to Ukraine emergency app
Residents in Kyiv also warned of chemical attack and street-to-street fighting in false message sent by unknown party
Unknown hackers have targeted Ukraine’s nationwide emergency alert mobile app, sending residents in Kyiv a warning that they were at risk of an imminent nuclear strike.
The app reported a high possibility of nuclear radiation late on Sunday. It also wrongly warned of a chemical threat to the Ukrainian capital and street-to-street fighting. The messages were written in English with spelling mistakes, as well as in Ukrainian.
Many residents ignored the alerts, which began shortly before 11pm local time, assuming that the app had been compromised. Others were scared. “I was briefly terrified,” one woman, Nina, said. “I lay on my bed and wondered what was coming.”
A message written in Russian also claimed Ukraine was about to be hit by Oreshnik missiles, which can carry nuclear warheads. The Kremlin has used the ballistic weapon three times before, hitting the Kyiv region and the cities of Dnipro and Lviv.
The false alerts on a smartphone. Photograph: AP In a post on Sunday, the Ukrainian emergency app said “unauthorised parties” had interfered with its operation. The channel had been temporarily suspended, it said, warning users not to click on links in “suspicious notifications”.
It was unclear on Monday who might have carried out the cyber-raid, or why. Russian officials claimed hackers had also sent fake emergency alerts there after gaining access to the app of the ministry for emergencies, based in Moscow.
One of their posts mentioned the hacking group Hitcore. Mash, a Russian Telegram channel with links to the security services, said it had spoken to representatives of Hitcore and that they had claimed responsibility for the attack. The report could not be verified.
The fake nuclear threats to Ukraine came as Russia resumed its attacks on the southern city of Kherson, hours after the end of a ceasefire during which hundreds of people were evacuated from the nearby Kremlin-controlled town of Oleshky.
Kherson’s military administration said a Russian drone hit a hospital at 7.40am. Video footage showed wrecked rooms, with windows blown out, doors broken, and debris on the street. Nobody was hurt, officials said.
There is evidence that the Russian army used the six-day ceasefire, which the White House said was brokered by the first lady, Melania Trump, to strengthen its positions in Oleskhy and to rotate in new troops. Bodies of dead civilians were also removed from a hospital morgue.
Footage shared with Sky News showed Russian soldiers deploying heavy military equipment and delivering ammunition. They carried large bags into burnt-out houses and buildings and disappeared into basements, the broadcaster reported.
Armoured vehicles were spotted moving around Oleshky’s streets. The occupied city is 3 miles from Kherson, on the opposite bank of the Dnipro River. Before last week’s truce, resupply was difficult because of the threat from Ukrainian kamikaze drones.
Ukraine defies Trump to resume attacks on Russian oil refineries
According to the commander of Ukraine’s 34th Separate Marine Brigade, Dmitry Pulinets, Russian soldiers were previously unable to drive in the city, “neither during the day, nor at night, nor in bad weather”.
“Now they have this opportunity. And for the last few days this movement has been happening constantly,” he told Sky News.
The ceasefire expired at 11pm on Sunday. Both sides hailed the local pause in the fighting – the most significant since 2022 – as a success. Ukraine’s ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, who visited Oleshky to coordinate the mission, said it could be repeated in other occupied cities in the Kherson region.
He declined to say how many Oleskhy residents had chosen to go to Ukraine and how many to Russia, citing an agreement with Moscow to keep the figure secret. Ukrainian media have reported that most of the evacuation buses headed to Ukraine through Crimea, from where a plane took them to Gomel, a city in Belarus. Melania Trump said in a post that more than 750 people had left.
Lubinets paid tribute to the US first lady and said he had been in daily contact with her via her aide Marc Beckman. He said he hoped to bring back some of the “thousands of people” who had disappeared, as well as prisoners of war and bodies retrieved last week from Oleshky’s morgue. There were millions of Ukrainian citizens living in occupied territory, he said.
Vladimir Putin’s spokesperson Dmitry Peskov, however, said on Monday that there were no immediate plans for another truce elsewhere. He said it was standard practice for army units to regroup in such circumstances and that he assumed Ukraine’s armed forces had done the same.
Meanwhile, officials in the western region of Vinnytsia said two civilians had been killed in a drone strike next to an education facility. The victims were a 13-year-old girl, who died at the scene from her injuries, and a woman, who died later in hospital. Several other children were wounded, the officials said.

items.content:
The Intel stock collapse is getting worse — and the $3.7 trillion chip rout is spreading
Wall Street mostly swept up last week's tech wreckage Monday. Chip stocks kept tracking mud back through the house.
About 7 in 10 S&P 500 stocks rose Monday, yet nearly every chip stock fell, and the group shed more than $400 billion in market value in a single session, by Yahoo Finance calculations.
This price reflects trading activity during the overnight session on the Blue Ocean ATS, available 8 PM to 4 AM ET, Sunday through Thursday, when regular markets are closed.
The chipmaker slid about 9% after its worst day since 1974 on Oct. 30, when a disappointing forecast knocked nearly 29% off the stock. Monday's close left Intel worth less than half of what it was when September ended.
Micron ( MU ), Sandisk ( SNDK ), Seagate ( STX ), and Western Digital ( WDC ) — the memory and storage names that led the chip boom this year — all got clobbered, falling roughly 6% to 8%. Marvell ( MRVL ) fell even harder, a drop that came as it agreed to buy Lumentum ( LITE ) in a $115 billion deal. Nvidia ( NVDA ) held up better than most, but it's still down about 16% since Oct. 6.
Intel, Marvell, AMD and the memory names led the chip rout, while Nvidia barely moved. · Yahoo Finance AlphaSpace Zoom out and the mess gets bigger. Chip and memory stocks have lost about $3.7 trillion in market value since Oct. 6, by Yahoo Finance calculations. Nvidia lost the most in dollars, but Intel's drop of nearly half is the steepest among the giants.
Yahoo Finance Not everything tied to AI bled. SpaceX ( SPCX ) rose, though it's still well below where it started October. Software was mixed, apart from cybersecurity stocks like Fortinet ( FTNT ) and CrowdStrike ( CRWD ), which fell with chips.
Adam Johnson, founder of the Bullseye Brief and portfolio manager of the American Ingenuity Fund, thinks last week's sell-off already priced in the worst.
"The market kitchen-sinked it," Johnson told Yahoo Finance on Monday. "They discounted everything that could go wrong. And when you do that, typically that's when you see a bottom."
John Chambers, founder and CEO of JC2 Ventures and Cisco's former CEO, expects the gap between winners and losers to keep widening.
"There will be major train wrecks," Chambers told Yahoo Finance, also on Monday. "And rising tide does not raise all boats. I would not bet against Nvidia."
Stock Trader's Almanac editor Jeff Hirsch, who coined the term " Octoberphobia ," bought the sell-off on Oct. 30. History is on his side. Chips have climbed in all eight midterm cycles since 1994, measured from the last October close through the following June, by Yahoo Finance calculations. But in 2002 and 2018, they first fell about another 11%.
Next up is AMD ( AMD ), which reports third quarter results Tuesday after the bell , the same day as the midterm vote.
"Historically, seasonally, it sets up great for this period of time, the best months of the year for semiconductors," Hirsch told Yahoo Finance on Oct. 30.

items.title: If hackers can take control of a supermarket freezer, how vulnerable is other tech?
items.summary: Dozens of shops across European countries have been hit by a cyber-attack affecting their fridges.
items.content:
Supermarkets across Europe have been hit by a suspected cyber-attack affecting their fridges and freezers, and raising concern about the vulnerabilities of internet-connected hardware from industrial machinery to humble domestic appliances.
Smart devices which are connected to the internet can include fridges, central heating, and even washing machines.
And while that makes them easier to control remotely, in theory, any device which goes online can potentially be exploited by malicious actors.
However, that doesn't mean hackers can easily take control of it, and big brands generally go to great lengths to make sure their tech is secure.
Exploits have been found before in some devices. In 2015, researchers demonstrated how a vulnerability in a Samsung smart fridge could allow them to intercept internet traffic.
But there's no evidence domestic appliances are being targeted in the cyber-attacks which targeted supermarkets in November.
Ciaran Martin, former chief executive of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) says manufacturers needed to do more to make connected devices secure.
"There's a lot more that we need to demand of big tech to give us safer devices and products in the first place," he said.
He advised consumers to keep devices updated and enable multi-factor authentication wherever possible.
"I know it's a pain, but it only takes a few seconds," he said.
Since April 2024, UK law has required manufacturers of certain consumer smart devices to meet minimum cyber security standards, including requirements around passwords and security updates.
The NCSC said it was working with international partners and industry to understand the supermarket incidents, but it was unaware of any impact on the UK.
However, researchers from UK Cyber Defence have identified more than 800 refrigeration and building-control interfaces associated with British retailers that can be accessed over the public internet.
That doesn't necessarily mean they can be hacked, but it could leave them exposed to attackers exploiting weak passwords or software vulnerabilities.
The government has already held talks with senior food retailers about cyber resilience, following earlier attacks on supermarkets.
Helen Dickinson, chief executive of the British Retail Consortium, has said cyber incidents are a major concern for retailers, with businesses working alongside the NCSC to share intelligence and strengthen their defences.
It would not be the first time that hacks have raised concern about impact on food supply.
When UK supermarkets M&S and the Co-op were targeted by ransomware hackers in May 2025, the retailers struggled to stock some shop shelves with fresh deliveries.
Customers across the UK complained of empty shelves in the days following the attack.
Tom Hegel, a researcher at cyber-security firm SentinelOne, said retailers must be clearer about responsibility.
"The question retailers need to answer is who owns the security of that equipment, not just who repairs it," he said.
He said internet connectivity can make everyday technology more convenient, but security needed to keep pace.
"Once an attacker can operate those controls, legitimate functions such as defrosting become tools for disruption," he said.
"Changing a setting can destroy physical stock, not just interrupt a computer system."
Could cars, power plants and water supplies be vulnerable?
Outside of the home, connected tech is used to remotely manage industrial machinery and vehicles.
Cyber security expert Ken Munro pointed to a 2015 demonstration in which researchers remotely hacked a Jeep through its internet-connected entertainment system, prompting improvements in vehicle security.
"Fortunately, the vehicle industry woke up to this and fixed the problem," he said.
Mobile connections are also widely used to monitor equipment in power plants and water networks, allowing engineers to manage systems remotely.
Munro said UK utilities were generally good at securing these connections, but standards varied around the world.
His biggest concern was smaller, poorly funded utility companies which may still be relying on older, vulnerable equipment.
Without proper protections, "any factory or equipment" connected to the internet - ranging from carmakers to electricity or transport infrastructure - could face similar risks, said Olivier Daloy, a cybersecurity expert at Zscaler.

The U.S. military faces “profound” long-term readiness concerns, one expert said.
By John Haltiwanger , a staff writer at Foreign Policy .

Growing signs suggest that U.S. President Donald Trump could restart the war with Iran following the U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday.
While there have been renewed diplomatic efforts to reach a deal over the past week, the terms Iran has put on the table—including lifting all U.S. sanctions—would be difficult for the United States to accept. Meanwhile, Trump has offered mixed signals on what he plans to do, indicating that he hasn’t yet made a decision. Over the weekend, Trump said the war could be over soon, but he also said that the U.S. still had to “take care” of one or two nuclear sites and would have to give Iran “the hammer” at some point.

Meanwhile, Trump has offered mixed signals on what he plans to do, indicating that he hasn’t yet made a decision. Over the weekend, Trump said the war could be over soon, but he also said that the U.S. still had to “take care” of one or two nuclear sites and would have to give Iran “the hammer” at some point.
The war has cost U.S. taxpayers an estimated $47.1 billion so far and has left the United States military depleted on a number of levels—from drastically reducing key munitions stockpiles to the destruction of expensive equipment and aircraft.
The U.S. is estimated to have used up to 65 percent of its Patriot air-defense interceptors and 80 percent of its Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) ballistic missile interceptors since the war began, for example. The U.S. stockpile of Tomahawk cruise missiles is estimated to have fallen from around 3,000 to 2,000 since the fighting started, and the war has reportedly left its stocks of missiles for the Army Tactical Missile Systems, or ATACMS, and precision strike missiles almost exhausted. Around a quarter of the U.S. military’s MQ-9 Reaper drones have also reportedly been lost during the war. Rebuilding these stockpiles will take years.
All of this raises questions about U.S. military readiness and capabilities if Trump chooses to return to war post-election.
The United States still has significant military capabilities in the Middle East, including over 50,000 troops and two aircraft carrier strike groups. Another aircraft carrier strike group is en route and should arrive near the end of this month.
Longer-range and more advanced capabilities like Tomahawk missiles are “significantly depleted,” and Patriot and THAAD batteries are “limited,” but there are “other ways for the president to be able to successfully execute the missions he’s looking at,” Jonathan Panikoff, the senior director of the Scowcroft Middle East Security Initiative at the Atlantic Council, told Foreign Policy .
“In the short term, the U.S. is likely quite ready to carry out the planned operations,” said Stacie Pettyjohn, a senior fellow and director of the defense program at the Center for a New American Security. An additional Patriot unit was sent from Texas to Israel, for instance, and the Pentagon has likely dispersed aircraft and personnel from bases that are very close to Iran and less well defended, such as in Bahrain and Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar, Pettyjohn said.
But that’s just the short term. The picture could change drastically over a longer time horizon.
“The long-term readiness concerns are quite profound,” Pettyjohn said. These constraints include “munitions stockpiles”—for example, long-range standoff attack missiles and defensive interceptors—“deferred ship maintenance, and disrupted readiness cycles, which affect what forces will be available for future contingencies.”
The U.S. has reportedly told Gulf allies to brace for a short but intense campaign targeting Iranian infrastructure and nuclear sites, with the goal of strengthening Washington’s negotiation position. But Trump has consistently struggled to dictate the direction of the war, and Iran has proved to be a resilient adversary. The U.S. and Israel conducted thousands of strikes on Iran, but Tehran has not budged in its demands. Iran has also exhibited an ability to quickly adapt its tactics and has proved that even with a diminished military, it can disrupt the flow of traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.
“If Iran has prepared for a more protracted campaign of attacks against U.S. forces in the region and civilian infrastructure, that could quickly drain near-term U.S. readiness. So overall, restarting the war would be a huge gamble,” Pettyjohn added.
Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei during a recent meeting with commanders reportedly said that Iran’s response would be “immediate, effective” and “without any geographical limitations.” Iran would likely move to strike U.S. bases in the region and energy facilities in Arab countries in response to the war restarting, but it has also signaled that a wider menu of civilian infrastructure could be targeted.
“It is impossible to defend everywhere,” Pettyjohn said. “The U.S. can in the short term surge fighter aircraft to help interdict incoming drones and to potentially suppress Iranian launchers, although the latter must fly over Iran and is at risk of being shot down. But that is a difficult posture to sustain indefinitely as aircraft are likely operating from more distant bases, flying long sorties, and require lots of tanker support.”
Resupplying forces that are under attack with additional weapons would be difficult as well, Pettyjohn said.
The decisions that Trump makes with regard to Iran will also have an impact on U.S. military capabilities in other theaters moving forward. The “more capabilities” that are used against Iran, Panikoff said, “the less that are available for other potential conflicts in the future.”

Keir Starmer visited China in January, the first trip by a British prime minister since Theresa May travelled there in 2018. Photograph: Carl Court/Reuters
Keir Starmer visited China in January, the first trip by a British prime minister since Theresa May travelled there in 2018. Photograph: Carl Court/Reuters
UK making up China policy ‘as it goes along’, MPs warn
Commons committee says lack of coherent strategy is hampering business and leaving national security risks unaddressed
The UK is making up policy on China “as it goes along” and risks having its strategy dictated by Washington or Beijing, a parliamentary report has concluded.
An investigation by the Commons business, innovation, science and trade select committee said Labour’s failure to formulate a coherent strategy since 2024 “combined the worst of both worlds” for the UK in relation to China.
Liam Byrne, Labour MP and chair of the committee said the UK’s policy on China meant it was also endangering its business with the EU with the risk of being “cut off” from big manufacuring contracts.
The government could neither deliver commercial opportunities to British businesses nor control the “increasing exposure to unquantified, managed risk” in relations with China, it found.
The report said: “In 2024, the new government promised a strategic, long-term, consistent UK approach to China. It has not delivered on this.
“Britain must shape its own relationship with China or risk having that relationship shaped for us in Washington or Beijing.”
The UK’s relationship with China has been marked by a lack of engagement in the last 10 years, with Keir Starmer making the first official visit in January since Theresa May in 2018.
That trip was billed as an effort to end the “diplomatic ice age”, but since 2018 China has benefited from an export boom that is now fuelling fears about deindustrialisation, adding to deep-seated existing concerns about cyber espionage and national security.
UK’s ‘incoherent’ approach to China plagued by lack of expertise, report says
The MPs acknowledged the advantages of trading with Beijing in their report, noting that British businesses have profitable operations in China and “are ambitious to grow” and learn from the country’s “world-leading” innovations.
At the same time, consumers benefit from low-cost imports when household incomes are squeezed, with electric vehicles being a case in point.
However, Byrne sharply criticised the government’s piecemeal approach.
“Britain’s businesses cannot plan for the future when the government keeps making up its China policy as it goes along.
“Ministers promised clarity and consistency. Instead, we have opportunities missed, risks unmanaged and decisions left until the 11th hour.”
The committee cited the decision in March to block the Chinese firm Ming Yang from building a £1.5bn wind energy plant in Scotland after years of negotiation because of unspecified security risks.
Scotland’s first minister, John Swinney, has called on Andy Burnham to reconsider Starmer’s decision.
That decision, along with the emergency takeover of British Steel from its Chinese owners, “has been characterised by reactivity, inconsistency and opacity”, the report said.
Work on a new strategy, the committee said, should be combined with official preparations for new trade remedies to counter unfair competition, including potential tariffs on EVs, something Downing Street has not ruled out.
The report calls for “clear new rules of the game” and recommends the designation of a “red zone” for industries that would be off-limits for Chinese investment and a “green zone”, where trade should be encouraged.
Byrne said a China strategy was an urgent concern as “Europe is changing fast” and “proposing new trade protections as it gets bolder with Beijing and warier of Washington”.
The new laws “may trap Britain outside EU trade walls, cutting us off from our largest market”.
Byrne said the government “should be prepared to consider dynamic alignment” with the EU include tariffs on EVs “as the price of securing British firms a place in the EU’s Made in Europe project” and to help guard against China dominance.
The UK is already under pressure to align with the EU on tariffs on EVs, but the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, has said he will make a decision in the best interests of the UK.
The EU has already imposed tariffs on Chinese EVs, capped the number of hybrid cars that can be imported from China and is now considering a Franco-German proposal for a “kill switch” to block imports if China weaponises trade – as it did last year with curbs on exports of rare-earth minerals and chips. “The UK’s partners are moving further and faster,” the report noted.
China is now on track to surpass last year’s record $1.19tn trade surplus with the rest of the world.
Its latest five-year plan, covering 2026 to 2030, gives a glimpse of where China is going next in prioritising the strategic expansion of high-value green exports such as EVs, batteries, wind turbines, hydrogen and solar panels.
A government spokesperson said it did not accept the committee’s verdict. “We recognise the committee’s work on this report, but we disagree with its conclusion.”
They added that the government’s approach was “consistent” - it cooperated where it could and challenged where it must.
“Our trade strategy makes clear that we will capitalise on every opportunity to grow our economy while never compromising on our national security, and our increased discussions with China allows us to directly raise concerns where they arise,” the spokesperson said.

RBA interest rates live updates: Michele Bullock at a press conference after the Reserve Bank of Australia raised the cash rate to 4.85%. Follow the latest news. Photograph: Dean Lewins/AAP
The RBA governor, Michele Bullock, says “this is not the news that many Australians want to hear, but it is what’s needed to get inflation down”.
She says “some pain now will prevent even worse pain down the track”.
I understand that today’s decision is going to be difficult for Australians with mortgages, many of whom are already managing large repayments.
But households with mortgages are not the only Australians doing it tough. Every household is dealing with higher prices for groceries, electricity, insurance, and other essentials.
High inflation is particularly painful for Australians on lower incomes, including people who rent and have little or no savings to fall back on.
The comments were made in opening remarks to journalists in Sydney ahead of questions.
Australian share market ends higher after RBA rate hike
Michele Bullock addresses media following rate hike decision
Chalmers plays down role of federal budget on inflation
Chalmers says rate hike will be ‘difficult news’ for Australians already paying 'hefty price'
Chalmers says Australians bracing for 'difficult decision'
The Australian stock market ended higher after the central bank did what it was expected to do and hiked interest rates for the fifth time this calendar year.
The main S&P/ASX200 index rose 30.3 points, or 0.3%, to 8886.8, as the broader All Ordinaries gained 31.7 points, or 0.4%, to 9008.9.
Most of the market’s 11 sectors were in the green, with the major materials and consumer stocks leading the way, while the energy sector carried most of the loss-makers.
The Reserve Bank board ended its two-day meeting on monetary policy on Tuesday with a 25 basis point rise in the cash interest rate to 4.85%.
The Australian dollar was buying 69.77 US cents, down from 70.21 US cents at 5pm on Monday.
Bullock asked about effect of US-Israel war in Iran on interest rates
Guardian Australia’s economics editor, Patrick Commins, asks Bullock whether the RBA would have raised rates if oil prices had stayed low.
In other words, what would have happened had the US and Israel not launched strikes against Iran?
Bullock gives a nuanced response, pointing out that Australia already had a problem with “excess demand” that required cooling.
Now, would that have meant that we had to go up the same amount? I don’t know the answer to that.
It’s possible that it’s caused interest rates to mean they have to be a little bit higher.
Bullock goes on to articulate an economic risk posed by raising inflation expectations caused by high oil prices: as consumers resign themselves to higher prices, businesses lift theirs ahead of anticipated rising costs, creating a self-fulfilling loop that entrenches inflation.
RBA independence from government ‘a two-way street’, Bullock says
Michele Bullock has described independence as a “two-way street”, noting that she doesn’t tell the government what to spend on, and that the government doesn’t tell the RBA what to do with rates.
The role of public sector spending in fuelling inflation looms large, with Labor under pressure from critics over five rate hikes this year.
Bullock says that governments need to decide on how much spending is required to provide for the nation. She says:
But that is for governments to decide. Independence is a two-way street. I don’t tell them what to do with fiscal policy. They don’t tell me what to do with interest rates.
Unemployment and housing concerns behind board split: RBA governor
The RBA decision to raise rates was split, with three members of the rate-setting board preferring a hold, while six voted to raise.
Bullock says those in favour of a hold were concerned about risks to the economy, including rising unemployment and housing weakness. Bullock said:
They felt that there were potential downside risks in these circumstances, particularly since we’d already done four interest rate rises, and maybe we should wait a bit longer to get some more data to test that.
Bullock says market watchers shouldn’t interpret the split decision as a sign the RBA won’t raise further if inflation risks materialise.
The RBA governor, Michele Bullock, says “this is not the news that many Australians want to hear, but it is what’s needed to get inflation down”.
She says “some pain now will prevent even worse pain down the track”.
I understand that today’s decision is going to be difficult for Australians with mortgages, many of whom are already managing large repayments.
But households with mortgages are not the only Australians doing it tough. Every household is dealing with higher prices for groceries, electricity, insurance, and other essentials.
High inflation is particularly painful for Australians on lower incomes, including people who rent and have little or no savings to fall back on.
The comments were made in opening remarks to journalists in Sydney ahead of questions.
Photograph: Jeremy Piper/Reuters Economists intrepret RBA’s decision
Several economists are interpreting the RBA’s statement accompanying the rate hike as “dovish”, which means further hikes are less likely.
UBS economists describe the decision as “clearly dovish” while Anthony Malouf , economist at Ebury, says there is an “absence of a clear tightening bias”.
The Australian dollar also immediately dropped against its US counterpart after the decision, which shows traders do not believe the central bank is, at this stage, looking to hike much further.
This could all change if inflation remains elevated, but for the moment, some economists and currency traders believe this could be the last hike, at least for a while.
Chalmers was asked about the federal budget and its impact on inflation. He said:
Our budgets are not what’s putting upward pressure on inflation. But we can play a helpful role and that’s what we intend to do.
Jim Chalmers , the treasurer, is speaking now after the RBA’s decision. He said:
Today’s decision was widely expected, but that doesn’t make it any easier for Australian families and businesses to absorb. It will be difficult news for many Australians who are already paying a hefty price for circumstances outside of their control.
He pointed to the ongoing war in the Middle East as a major factor in inflation:
The war’s in its ninth month and its re-escalation is putting sustained upward pressure on inflation.
It’s weighing on growth and its end can’t come soon enough for the global economy or for Australians facing cost of living pressures.
Jim Chalmers. Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAP Macquarie Bank announces it will pass rate rise on
Macquarie Bank has already announced it will pass on the interest rate rise to mortgage holders.
The bank said it will increase variable home loans by 0.25%, effective 19 November. It will also increase ongoing variable rates paid on its transactions and savings accounts by 0.25%, a boon to savers. Ben Perham , the head of personal banking, said:
With household budgets already feeling the strain, today’s decision by the RBA will be challenging for many Australians.
To help our variable home loan customers prepare, we’re again waiting more than two weeks before this latest increase takes effect.
Photograph: David Gray/Reuters The cash rate is now the highest it has been in 18 years
A chart showing the cash rate The decision was not a unanimous one: six members of the RBA board voted to raise the cash rate, while three voted to leave it unchanged.
The Board is conscious of the period in which inflation has been too high. Given the revised inflation outlook and the continuing upside risks, the Board judged that a further tightening in financial conditions is warranted to support the return of inflation to target.
The Board will continue to do what it considers necessary to bring inflation sustainably back to target.

US Stock Market Fails To Recover as $700 Billion Comeback Collapses
Wall Street appeared ready to recover from October's $2 trillion technology stock wipeout on Monday. Within hours, roughly $700 billion in fresh market gains had evaporated.
The S&P 500 surged as much as 1.1% in morning trading before closing down 0.5%. The Nasdaq Composite fell 1.1%, extending last week's brutal AI stock selloff.
The reversal came shortly after CNBC host Jim Cramer posted on X:
He was referring to Marvell's $115 billion acquisition of Lumentum. But the timing quickly revived jokes about Cramer's famously mixed market predictions.
Oil prices dropped to $104 as possible US-Iran peace talks raised hopes of cheaper energy and easing inflation.
Stocks initially jumped. The Nasdaq 100 gained around 1.3%, while the Dow climbed more than 1%.
But investors soon returned to the same concern that erased more than $2 trillion from the Nasdaq 100 during October: How much longer can Big Tech keep spending billions on AI without delivering sufficient returns?
Oracle plunged nearly 9% after announcing plans to raise $20 billion through stock and bond sales to fund its AI expansion. Marvell lost almost 13%.
Meanwhile, White House economic adviser Kevin Hassett dismissed fears of an AI financing crisis.
"There's so much cash in the ecosystem that I think that people should be reassured," Hassett said.
Interestingly, nearly 70% of S&P 500 companies finished higher. The weakness remained concentrated in major technology stocks.
As for Cramer's supposed curse, the Inverse Cramer ETF, designed to bet against his recommendations, lost 15% before closing in 2024.
Investors now face Tuesday's US midterm elections and Friday's jobs report, with confidence in the AI trade already shaken.

items.title: Apple unsure when more foldable iPhones will be available after selling out
items.summary: Apple’s foldable iPhone Duo was a hit with people willing to spend $2,000 on a new mobile.
items.content:
The new head of Apple says the company is working to get its new foldable iPhones available to more people after the $1,999 smartphone quickly sold out when it was released just over a week ago.
John Ternus, who in September took over the role as Apple's chief executive from Tim Cook, said on Monday that he was "thrilled" at the early reaction to the iPhone Duo.
While the costly phone, which sells for Â£1,999 in the UK, immediately sold out, some buyers have seen their screens crack .
The phones are still in high demand and Sabhi Kahn, Apple's new chief operating officer, said the technology giant did not know when more Duos would be available.
"At this time, it's really hard to predict when supply and demand will be in balance," Kahn said during a call with financial analysts to discuss Apple's latest financial results.
Apple executives did not mention during the call any issues with the iPhone Duo. But last week, the company said it would replace any phones that were impacted by an issue that caused a "small number" of the new phones to crack along the inside fold.
Nevertheless, Apple said on Monday that over the last year it sold more iPhones globally than it ever has before.
During the three months to 26 September, which did not include sales of the iPhone Duo that went on sale toward the end of October, Apple saw iPhone sales rise 17% to $57bn.
Apple has boasted throughout the year that iPhone sales have been surging, despite the company's warnings that crucial components for the device, along with Mac computers and iPads, were constrained to the point of weighing down sales.
Sales of Mac computers also grew during the quarter by 27%, hitting $10.7bn, another record for Apple.
Overall sales at the company rose by 15% for the year, to $479bn.
However, sales for both the iPad and Apple's wearable products, including its headphones and Watch fell by 10% and 7%, respectively.
Kahn noted during the call that most Apple devices are still seeing supply constraints driven in part by difficulty in getting enough microprocessors with "advanced nodes."
Those components are essentially computer chip technology that allows Apple's devices to operate more quickly, most of which Apple has manufactured through TSMC, which is based in Taiwan.
Khan said that such supply constraints are expected to continue into next year, particularly impacting iPads and Macs. The situation has been made worse by what the company has repeatedly insisted is "unexpected demand" for its products.
Ternus noted, too, that Apple is still seeing "unprecedented" cost increases for memory, or the ability of Apple devices to store data like apps, photos, and text messages.
Much of that memory storage runs through data centres which have seen a huge boom in demand for space as artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots and platforms, including those developed by OpenAI and Anthropic, have become popular.
As demand for memory has grown, storage prices have gone up for tech companies like Apple.
Cook had earlier this year referred to the sudden increase in data centre costs that Apple was seeing as a "thousand year flood."
It has led to the company raising prices on essentially all of its hardware products by around 20%.

Rendering of offshore LNG liquefaction and export plant
ST LNG is proposing to build an LNG export plant off the coast of Texas in East Matagorda Bay.
The US Maritime Administration (MARAD) on Oct. 28 approved ST LNG LLC's application for a deepwater port license for an $8.2-billion LNG export plant planned about 10.4 miles offshore Matagorda County, Tex.
MARAD said construction would begin in 2027 with in-service in 2029. At full capacity of 8.4 million tonnes/year (tpy), the plant would include 20 fixed offshore platforms, 4 LNG floating storage units, 4 mooring systems, 4 liquefaction systems, and 7.7 miles of pipeline. ST LNG expects to develop the project in 4 independent phases, each with a nominal liquefaction capacity of 2.1-million tpy.
The approval clears a major federal regulatory hurdle, but ST LNG still must meet outstanding federal and state requirements, secure customer commitments, arrange financing and reach a final investment decision. The privately held company's proposed plant would be its first LNG export project.
ST LNG plans to obtain feed gas from the Tres Palacios Natural Gas Storage and Trading Hub and the Williams Markham Gas Processing Plant through an existing 36-in. OD Transcontinental Gas Pipe Line (Transco) pipeline about 5.6 miles northeast of the port. The project includes a proposed 5.6-mile pipeline lateral connecting the offshore plant to the existing pipeline, along with 2.1 miles of interconnecting pipelines between the four phases.
MARAD said it completed the project's Final Environmental Impact Statement in 410 days, about 3.7 years faster than the historical average. The agency called it the fastest deepwater port license review in more than 20 years.
In a statement, MARAD Administrator Stephen M. Carmel said ST LNG represents the Trump administration's third deepwater port license approval.
The US Department of Energy on Apr. 22 authorized ST LNG to export LNG equivalent to 460 bcf/year of natural gas to countries with which the US has qualifying free trade agreements (FTA). DOE is separately reviewing the company's request to export LNG to non-FTA countries.

items.content:
Why the Treasury General Account Impairs Federal Reserve Operational Independence
Large Treasury Account Balances at the Fed are shaping how monetary policy is being conducted
Since Kevin Warsh took office as chairman of the Federal Reserve, the size of the Fed’s balance sheet has come under renewed scrutiny. The roughly $1 trillion Treasury General Account (TGA) at the Fed is a major obstacle to reducing it under the current monetary framework. Treasury chooses how much cash to hold, but the Fed must manage the effect of that choice on bank reserves. This can be seen as fiscal authority infringing upon the independence of the central bank since Treasury’s cash-management priorities help determine the minimum size of the Fed’s balance sheet.
The TGA functions as Treasury’s primary checking account and is held at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. At the end of September 2026, it held $984 billion, making it one of the Fed’s largest liabilities, alongside bank reserves and currency in circulation. Unlike reserves, the Fed does not pay interest on the TGA balance.

Until 2008, Treasury held much of its cash in Treasury Tax and Loan accounts (TT&L) at commercial banks. These deposits earned interest at 25 basis points below the effective federal funds rate. Keeping Treasury cash at commercial banks also prevented many tax payments from draining reserves out of the banking system. But when the effective federal funds rate fell below 25 basis points in late 2008, the TT&L interest formula turned negative. Treasury moved balances into the TGA. As the Fed expanded reserves, it became easier to accommodate a larger and more variable Treasury balance at the central bank.
According to Treasury, the TGA is a buffer. Its cash policy, adopted in 2015, calls for a balance sufficient to meet at least one week of projected needs, including maturing marketable debt, so that it can continue paying its obligations if borrowing is temporarily disrupted. The scale is substantial: Treasury said in 2025 that weekly cash needs can exceed $800 billion around certain payment dates.
The buffer also gives Treasury room to operate during debt-limit confrontations. During debt-limit suspensions, the Treasury can raise debt through auctions to increase its TGA balance. Even though the 2023 law suspending the debt limit specifically restricted borrowing to create an unusually large balance before that suspension expired, the Treasury still increased the TGA balance from $23.4 billion to $721.9 billion during the suspension.
Suppose debt outstanding is $35 trillion, and Treasury holds $800 billion in the TGA when the limit begins to bind. It can draw on that cash to make payments. Once Congress restores borrowing capacity, Treasury can issue debt to rebuild its normal cash balance. The Treasury’s need for cash before, during, and after a debt-limit impasse produces large swings in an account on the Fed’s balance sheet.
Those swings are transmitted to bank reserves. Taxes and Treasury auctions that increase the TGA generally decrease reserves as payments move from private bank accounts to Treasury’s account at the Fed. When Treasury spends the money, the flow reverses. Seasonal variation in receipts and outlays adds to the movement.
A change in the TGA need not change the total size of the Fed’s balance sheet; it can change its composition instead. If the TGA rises by $500 billion while Fed assets and other liabilities remain constant, reserves fall by $500 billion. That matters because the Fed relies on interest on reserves balances (IORB) as its primary policy tool to keep short-term rates near its target. When reserves are plentiful, a TGA-driven decline has little effect on rates. When reserves approach scarcity, the same decline can push rates upward. After a debt-limit impasse ended in 2019, the TGA rose by roughly $140 billion in the third quarter; Fed staff linked the consequent reserve drain to volatility in money-market rates.
The solution under the current ample-reserves framework is to keep a reserve buffer large enough that Treasury cash flows do not push the banking system into scarcity. That places a floor under balance-sheet reduction, with reserves having to be ample enough to ensure that TGA induced shifts do not move reserve balances outside of its regime range. Using the Fed’s own graph on the ample-reserves regime shown above, excessive balance sheet reduction could cause shifts in the TGA to periodically shift the quantity of reserves left of A, outside of the A-B ample reserve regime range.
Here the hierarchy of priorities becomes clear. Treasury maintains a large cash balance to protect its ability to pay. The Fed then holds additional assets and reserves to accommodate the volatility that balance creates. Fiscal cash management is setting a constraint on monetary-policy implementation.
That constraint is a consequence of the present arrangement, not a law of central banking. Treasury could again place some collateralized balances at commercial banks. The Fed could offset TGA swings through changes in its bill holdings or lending operations. Each option has costs, and the choice among them is a choice about who bears the burden of Treasury’s cash flows. As long as the Fed relies on a large standing reserve buffer, Treasury’s preference for a large, flexible TGA will continue to dictate part of the size of the Fed’s balance sheet. A chairman who wants a smaller balance sheet will find that he can’t get one without the Treasury’s cooperation. That is the independence problem the balance-sheet debate has to confront.
